etymologies.etymologyHTML: Uncertain; probably a collateral form of brusque, but compare Irish briosc, Scottish Gaelic brisg, Welsh brys.

definitions.definition: Full of liveliness and activity; characterized by quickness of motion or action.

quote.citation: 1918, Norman Lindsay, The Magic Pudding, Sydney: Angus and Robertson, page 10:
quote.text: On such occasions he would remark--"Shaving may add an air that's somewhat brisker,For dignity, commend me to the whisker."

quote.citation: 2012 December 29, Paul Doyle, “Arsenal's Theo Walcott hits hat-trick in thrilling victory over Newcastle”, in The Guardian‎[2]:
quote.text: Ba, who has been linked with a January move to Arsenal, should have rewarded their brisk start with the opening goal in the 16th minute.

definitions.definition: Full of spirit of life; effervescing.

quote.citation: 1896, A. E. Housman, “Terence, this is stupid stuff”, in A Shropshire Lad:
quote.text: Why, if 'tis dancing you would be, / There's brisker pipes than poetry.

definitions.definition: Abrupt, curt in one's manner or in relation to others.

quote.citation: 1919, W[illiam] Somerset Maugham, “chapter 15”, in The Moon and Sixpence, [New York, N.Y.]: Grosset & Dunlap Publishers […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Her manner was brisk, and her good-breeding scarcely concealed her conviction that if you were not a soldier you might as well be a counter-jumper.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive, often with "up") To make or become lively; to enliven; to animate.
